narrative:
The model estimates a 37% chance that you will not pass your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed one class in the past. While almost every student who ultimately passed had zero previous failures, your history of one failure strongly pulled the model toward expecting you to struggle again. This single piece of information had more influence than anything else.

Two other factors worked in your favor and partially offset that risk. First, your family has three or fewer members, which is less common among students who passed (only 34.5% of passers came from families this small). The model sees smaller families as slightly protective, perhaps because they can offer more focused support. Second, you have a clear ambition to pursue higher education, something every single student who passed also shared. This goal nudged the prediction back toward passing, though not enough to overcome the impact of your past failure.

To improve, focus on breaking the pattern of previous academic setbacks. With your strong desire to continue studying and the extra support remedial courses will provide, use this as an opportunity to build consistent study habits early. Even modest increases in weekly study time could make a real difference in turning that 37% risk into a passing outcome.
